newsitem.title: JAPAN: Deutsche Telekom satisfied with Tokyo share debut.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche Telekom satisfied with Tokyo share debut.

text.p: Officials of German telecoms giant Deutsche Telekom expressed satisfaction on Wednesday at its Tokyo stock market debut, although the share failed to match first-day rises in other bourses.
The world's third-largest telecoms firm had opened at 2,500 yen ($22) on the foreign stocks section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE) on Tuesday amid heavy trading.
"The listing here on the Tokyo Stock Exchange is especially important for us," Deutsche Telekom chief executive Ron Sommer told a news conference in Tokyo.
"From the very beginning, being present here in Asia's number one financial centre is a cornerstone for our globalisation strategy," he added.

The shares listed in Frankfurt on Tuesday at 28.5 marks and ended at 33.90 marks. Trade on Wall Street was also lively, with the issue soaring 14 percent to close 2-39/64 above Sunday's pricing at $21-1/2 in volume of 17 million shares.

But in contrast with Frankfurt and New York, the shares failed to rise in Tokyo, where they were eroded by profit-taking and ended 60 yen down at 2,440 yen. On Wednesday, the second day of trade, the share fell as low as 2,380 yen before closing at 2,410 yen.

"If you look to our offering price of 28.5 marks we have an excellent premium on our stock price, even in Tokyo, so we are not worried about the stabilising process," said Joachim Kroeske, chief finance officer.
"The first day's real price will be found and we're sure we can increase the price and stabilise in the next few days."
Telekom officials said 713 million shares were issued worldwide.
Of the 41 million shares that went to Asia, 20 percent were bought by Japanese institutional investors, Kroeske said.

The overhwelming popularity of the shares spurred the firm to issue an extra 100 million shares worldwide at the 11th hour. But Sommer stressed that despite the increase, there were no plans to alter the originally planned dividends.

Deutsche Telekom's TSE listing is the first by a European or U.S. company since 1993. Nearly five years ago, shares of 127 foreign firms were traded, but low liquidity, huge listing costs and currency fluctuations have driven many firms away.
So far this year, 11 firms have delisted in Tokyo, and after Exxon Corp leaves in December, only 66 will be left, TSE officials said earlier.
Some brokers said serious Japanese investors were participating in Telekom trade in Frankfurt and New York, staying away from the Tokyo market, which they said lacks liquidity.
Asked by reporters if the dilapidated foreign stocks section in Tokyo was a concern, Sommer brushed off the anxiety.
"The IPO of Deutsche Telekom in many respects is a first, so why shouldn't it make the first difference here?" he said. "We are very optimistic about the TSE."
